Visual metaphors are a unique form of human expression that combine visual elements with abstract ideas, and are commonly used in advertising and art. Despite their frequent appearance, visual metaphors have not been extensively researched in the field of computer vision. This paper proposes a new dataset and task called MetaCLUE, which is designed to help researchers better understand visual metaphors. The dataset includes a large collection of visual metaphors that are annotated with both quantitative and qualitative information. For each metaphor, researchers can provide a numerical score to represent its level of metaphorical meaning, as well as a text description of the underlying idea. This new dataset and task aim to provide a more comprehensive framework for studying visual metaphors. We also introduce a new model called MetaCLUE, which is designed to learn the underlying ideas and metaphorical structure of visual metaphors. The model is trained on the new dataset and can generate text descriptions of the underlying ideas, as well as their relationships. Experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy. Additionally, we conduct a user study to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model. The dataset and model are made publicly available to facilitate further research. Our research marks an important milestone in the field of visual metaphor research, and we hope that it will inspire a new wave of interest in this area. The art of video editing is a complex and time-consuming process that requires a deep understanding of storytelling and the ability to craft engaging narratives. In an effort to address these limitations, we have created a comprehensive video editing dataset consisting of 1,000 videos and 8,000 edits, accompanied by a benchmark suite that includes 7 tasks to assess the capabilities of AI models. Our dataset and benchmark suite provide a foundation for researchers to develop more effective video editing AI systems. Moreover, we have established a baseline for each task using a simple neural network and propose several novel techniques to improve AI-assisted video editing, including the use of pre-training, self-supervision, and self-adaptive learning. Our work marks a significant milestone in the field of video editing AI, and we hope that it will inspire further research and the development of more sophisticated video editing systems. We introduce antichain encryption, a novel encryption technique grounded in hypergraph theory, where a random encryption key is represented as a subset of symbols assigned randomly from designated antichain families. We demonstrate the efficacy of antichain encryption, showing it is both computationally secure and efficient, with communication and computation requirements scaling independently of key size. Additionally, antichain encryption offers the benefit of being usable offline, facilitated by its connection to hypergraph matching, which admits efficient approximation algorithms. We further explore specialized variants of antichain encryption, including a quantum-secure variant and an encryption method utilizing only 4-bit keys. The development of antichain encryption relies on establishing relationships between hypergraphs and antichains, as well as introducing a hypergraph matching conjecture that, if proven, would have significant implications for hypergraph matching. This work also touches upon potential applications of antichain encryption, including decentralized and energy-efficient encryption systems. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of antichain encryption, highlighting its connections to other encryption techniques and the potential for future research in this area. OctApps is a suite of tools designed for continuous gravitational-wave detection, which can be obtained through a standard Octave installation or a virtual environment. These tools facilitate the creation of time-frequency maps, noise estimation in frequency domain, and signal search in binary pulsars, as well as data enhancement through whitening and template template transformation. As a result of its open-source nature, users can customize the software to suit their specific research needs. We introduce a novel approach to enhancing the quality of circuit designs optimized by SAT solvers. Our method leverages a modified SAT proof to refine and improve target circuits while maintaining their original functionality. In contrast to previous techniques that utilize SAT proofs to identify flaws in designs, we shift the focus towards exploiting the proof to enhance existing, near-optimal designs. Our experiments demonstrate that even relatively low-quality proof certificates can serve as a basis for significantly improving circuit design. Furthermore, we show that using multiple SAT proofs in a hierarchical manner can be an effective strategy for further enhancing the design. Our method has been thoroughly tested on a diverse set of ISCAS'89 benchmarks, with the results consistently yielding enhanced designs. In some instances, the optimized designs matched optimal designs found through exhaustive searches. In other cases, the improvements were substantial, with one instance showcasing a 25.6x better design. Our findings suggest that SAT-based design optimization has the potential to produce highly competitive results, even when working with low-quality proof certificates. Moreover, we believe that our approach can be adapted to other verification tasks that rely on SAT proofs. To facilitate further research, we have made our source code available for public use. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the design enhancement process, highlighting the key factors that contribute to the quality of the optimized designs. Our study also explores the relationship between the design quality and the characteristics of the proof certificates used. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our research and propose several avenues for future investigation. Scientific publications are often analyzed using citation metrics, which provide valuable insights into the impact of individual papers or the quality of articles within specific fields. However, a common challenge arises when interpreting these metrics, as it can be difficult to identify the underlying cause of citation counts. To address this issue, a new method is proposed that utilizes citation metrics to generate personalized recommendations for scientific publications. This Recommender System takes into account a query paper, citating papers, and citation metrics as key inputs to estimate the likelihood of future citations for related publications. The system is demonstrated using an extensive dataset of 728,000 papers from the European Patent Office, which is representative of early-stage innovation. To evaluate the effectiveness of the Recommender System, a set of 1,500 papers was manually annotated, resulting in a high accuracy of 0.9. The method's ability to accurately predict future citations is then validated using an independent test set of 1,500 papers, which yielded a 0.2 correlation coefficient with actual citations received. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with existing methods is conducted, which shows that the proposed Recommender System outperforms the state-of-the-art in predicting citations. The method's versatility is also highlighted, as it can be applied to a wide range of citation-based recommender systems. This study introduces a new method for evaluating the effectiveness of base and detail components in image decomposition, by utilizing specific types of artifacts as performance metrics. We analyze how various filters, including Bayesian spectral radius, hard thresholding, nearby group hard thresholding, and others, perform in these tasks. We observe that these methods, despite their simplicity, do not consistently outperform more advanced approaches that employ sparsity promoting regularization or other sophisticated techniques in image decomposition. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm for optimizing the base and detail components of an image decomposition, by minimizing the total artifact measure. Through a range of experiments, our results show that this algorithm can yield improved results compared to existing methods, including those that rely on sparsity promoting constraints. We also propose an extension of this algorithm, which can be used to estimate the optimal parameters for more advanced techniques that employ L1 regularization. The findings of this study suggest that image decomposition can be effectively tackled using a straightforward algorithm, which does not require the incorporation of sparsity promoting constraints. We provide an open-source implementation of our method in the MATLAB package ArtiDec. The package can be accessed at https://github.com/abraham-yashar/ArtiDec. Acquiring reading comprehension skills is a crucial aspect of language learning, 
yet many English as a Second Language (ESL) students often find it difficult to 
process and comprehend written texts. To address this challenge, we have 
developed Sentence Completion Question (SC-Ques), a dataset consisting of 
sentences with missing information, requiring test-takers to provide the 
missing elements. This type of question assesses a reader's ability to extract 
key details from a text and has been found to be an effective way to evaluate 
reading comprehension. Based on our preliminary research, we created SC-Ques 
using authentic texts from Project Gutenberg and consulted ESL experts to ensure 
the questions' accuracy and difficulty. We then tested SC-Ques with 1,200 ESL 
students and discovered notable variations in their reading comprehension 
strategies. Furthermore, we compared our findings with those of a similar 
dataset, sentence completion questions from SAT and GRE. The results indicate 
that SC-Ques is a reliable tool for evaluating reading comprehension skills in 
ESL students. The SC-Ques dataset is available at https://github.com/zhujinyu/sc-ques.

The primary objective of reinforcement learning is to develop an agent capable of
acquiring rewards through interactions with an environment. This can be achieved
either through supervised training or by having the agent autonomously learn
from its environment. This research introduces the Unsupervised Reward Learning
Benchmark (URLB), a comprehensive evaluation framework comprising 28 tasks
divided into three categories: navigation, skill development, and game-based
challenges. This standardized test aims to assess the effectiveness of reward
learning methods in adapting to novel settings and tasks. This study provides an
in-depth analysis of the URLB, presenting baseline results and evaluating the
robustness of different reward learning techniques. Furthermore, the accompanying
code and URLB dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/DeepMind/urlb. This
research marks a significant milestone in the development of standardized
evaluation frameworks within the reinforcement learning community. By establishing
URLB, the research community can now efficiently compare and advance the
efficacy of reward learning techniques. This achievement is a result of the
collaborative efforts of numerous researchers from multiple organizations. We
hope that this benchmark will serve as a valuable resource for the community,
enabling the creation of more reliable and adaptable reward learning methods
that can be applied to a wide range of complex tasks. The study's code and
URLB dataset are available at https://github.com/DeepMind/urlb. This research also
includes supplementary materials, including video content, at https://youtu.be/8qQ8k8Q8k8.

We introduce a novel dataset, known as DarkMatch, comprising 2D image pairs of real, low-light scenes. The purpose of this dataset is to evaluate the effectiveness of various techniques for matching keypoint features in low-light conditions. The creation of this dataset was motivated by the observation that existing benchmark datasets, which utilize synthetic low-light transformations, do not adequately represent the challenges posed by real-world low-light imaging. To gather the dataset, we developed a portable setup for capturing low-light image pairs and manually annotated the correspondences between them. We also provide a baseline evaluation of different feature matching techniques on DarkMatch and compare them to results from well-known benchmark datasets. The ultimate goal of this research is to stimulate further study on this critical issue. Data and annotations can be found at https://github.com/berndpfrommer/DarkMatch. Deep neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples that can be crafted with relative ease. To mitigate this issue, adversarial training has been employed, typically involving the generation of adversarial samples through gradient-based methods like FGSM. However, such approaches often fail to produce high-quality adversarial samples, especially when the gradient is not well-defined, like in the case of ReLU activations. This paper presents a novel adversarial training method called LADDER, which generates adversarial samples by maximizing a target loss function. By incorporating a latent boundary constraint, LADDER can identify optimal solutions even when the gradient is not available. Experimentally, LADDER outperforms other methods in generating high-quality adversarial samples, resulting in improved robust standard and adversarial accuracies on various datasets. Furthermore, LADDER's effectiveness is demonstrated in the context of semi-supervised learning and domain adaptation tasks. To facilitate widespread adoption, LADDER's source code has been made publicly available. This research has the potential to advance the field of adversarial training and contribute to the development of more robust deep learning models. Additionally, LADDER's general approach can be applied to other optimization problems, like clustering and generative tasks, given the right loss function and constraints. We examine the algebraic properties of the Weierstrass $\sigma$-function, focusing on the case where algebraic dependencies exist among the j-invariants of elliptic curves over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. Given that the number of distinct j-invariants is limited, we investigate how these dependencies influence the behavior of $\sigma$-functions defined over such curves. By adapting a strategy initially developed by Klein and Macbeal, we establish new results regarding the algebraic nature of $\sigma$-products and $\sigma$-sums, which may contribute to the understanding of Galois groups associated with fields of rational functions and elliptic curves with finite periods. Our findings are illustrated through various examples, including a specific case involving the j-invariant $j = 0$ and its connection to the number theory of the rational numbers. Additionally, we explore the possibility of extending these results to a broader class of quasielliptic curves with finite periods. This research may also be relevant to the study of transcendental numbers, as we discuss how our results on $\sigma$-products and $\sigma$-sums can be used to establish bounds on the algebraic nature of Weierstrass $\sigma$-functions defined over specific algebraic curves. This, in turn, may contribute to the development of new algorithms for determining whether a given Weierstrass $\sigma$-function is algebraic or transcendental. Ultimately, we outline several open problems and areas for future research in this field. The corresponding Python code implementing these results is also provided. This method, which we call the statistical strength of functional connectivity (SSFC), measures the overall signal-to-noise ratio of a network and can be used to assess the accuracy of brain connectivity estimates. Furthermore, we have shown that our method can be used to predict the accuracy of brain connectivity estimates and can even be used when data from some sites are missing.  This method can be used to improve the reliability and accuracy of brain connectivity estimates in studies involving multiple sites with varying data quality. GANs have become a popular solution for generating synthetic data in various machine learning applications. However, their effectiveness heavily relies on the stability of the training process, which is often marred by the "mode collapse" problem. This issue arises when the model fails to capture the diverse characteristics of the underlying data distribution. To address this, our research investigates mode collapse by examining the Hessian matrix of the generator, revealing a connection between mode collapse and Hessian eigenvalues. Our method was tested on various datasets, and the results show that it outperforms existing mode collapse detection techniques. Additionally, our study provides insights into how mode collapse can be addressed by manipulating the generator's architecture. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of mode collapse and offers a novel solution to detect it. Existing research has primarily focused on creating these backdoors within models that can be accessed and modified. Our research focuses on a specific type of black-box attack called DeepPayload, which utilizes a neural payload injected into a deep learning model to create the desired backdoor. Unlike other backdoor attacks, DeepPayload is capable of launching attacks even after the model has been trained, making it a more challenging vulnerability to fix. We evaluate the effectiveness of DeepPayload by testing it on several models and datasets, and demonstrate its ability to successfully deceive models with a high degree of accuracy. To effectively plan power systems, a thorough understanding of system behavior under various conditions is necessary. This can be achieved by analyzing a large number of system scenarios in detail. However, directly studying each scenario is impractical due to the vast number of combinations. Instead, we propose a method to select a limited, representative set of scenarios that effectively capture the system's behavior across all combinations. This is made possible by utilizing autoencoders to reduce the complexity of power system states, allowing us to identify key features that distinguish each scenario. By selecting the most representative scenarios based on these features, we can create a diverse set of combinations. This approach has been successfully demonstrated on the IEEE 118-bus system. By using a small set of 15 representative scenarios, we can accurately simulate the system's behavior with a mean error of 0.96 and 2.01 for voltage and angle, respectively. This approach can also be applied to larger systems, such as the 3006-bus system, resulting in a small set of 50 representative scenarios that capture the system's behavior with a mean error of 0.99 and 1.99 for voltage and angle, respectively. The results show that the proposed method can effectively reduce the complexity of system analysis without compromising accuracy. This approach can also be used to select a small set of system states that capture the system's behavior under a specific criterion. Our research introduces a novel approach to converting existing sparse matrix
manipulation code into more efficient, vectorized forms. This method leverages
compiler optimizations, including loop transformations and vectorization, by
identifying and breaking down dependencies within the code using a technique
called trace analysis. We have developed a formal method for analyzing these
dependencies and have introduced a new optimization technique that can be
applied to a wide range of sparse matrix computations. This technique is able
to improve the vectorization efficiency of existing sparse matrix routines by
up to 90%. Furthermore, we have integrated our approach into the Clang compiler
toolchain and have demonstrated its effectiveness on a range of real-world
applications. One such application is the sparse matrix solver PARDIS, for which
we have achieved a 6.7x improvement in vectorization efficiency. This improvement
resulted in a 2.5x speedup in performance on a Skylake processor when running on
large-scale problems involving 1.5 million non-zero elements. In addition to
our approach, we have also developed a set of benchmarks designed to push the
limits of vectorized performance in sparse matrix computations. These benchmarks
are intended to provide a valuable resource for compiler developers and application
programmers who are working to optimize sparse matrix code for modern hardware.

The performance of these networks is assessed in three scenarios: when training and target data are available in full, when only target data is available, and when neither is accessible. To simulate domain shifts, images are manipulated to create synthetic datasets using techniques such as rotation, zoom, and noise injection. The study also employs adversarial domain adaptation methods, adversarial domain adaptation with selective backward propagation, and adversarial domain adaptation with selective backward propagation and entropy minimization. The outcomes of these techniques are compared to those of standard deep neural networks trained on full data, as well as those adapted to the target domain using standard deep learning methods. The study reveals that while domain adaptation methods can mitigate the effects of domain shifts, they do not consistently outperform standard deep learning techniques, and that the choice of network architecture is more critical than the specific domain adaptation method employed. The study also shows that the performance of deep learning techniques is more resilient to domain shifts when training data is available, and that the absence of target data significantly impairs network performance. The study's findings are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers working on deep learning techniques for image recognition tasks. Feature switches are a widely used method for managing diverse features in software development, but their impact on project health is not yet fully understood. This study examines the relationship between the adoption of feature switches and key project health metrics, including commit activity, code changes, and defect reports, across 14 influential Linux kernel projects and 1,103 feature switches in the Linux kernel repository. Our analysis reveals that enabling or disabling feature switches leads to an initial spike in code commits, followed by a decline, and shows that feature switches receive fewer bug reports than other parts of the project. Notably, feature switches receive an average of 0.55 defect reports per year, significantly fewer than other project elements. Our findings are consistent when accounting for project size and other factors. Our research offers valuable insights to developers and tool architects on the role of feature switches in software development. Pandemics have a profound impact on daily life and their management requires a multifaceted approach, involving both short-term and long-term planning. Effective pandemic response relies on a range of factors, including the availability of treatments, the transmission characteristics of the disease, the availability of testing and vaccination, infrastructure, economic stability, and social cohesion. As a result, pandemic models must be adaptable to changing information and data. This article will explore the importance of data-driven decision-making in pandemic response and planning, highlighting the crucial role of data in shaping our understanding of the pandemic and informing policy and personal decisions. We will also discuss the challenges of managing real-time data analysis and model updates, particularly in scenarios where data is scarce, fragmented, or difficult to analyze. Finally, we will outline the opportunities and challenges presented by the increasing availability of digital data and the need for robust data governance and infrastructure in informing and shaping pandemic response. Our goal is to emphasize the need for a comprehensive and inclusive data ecosystem that can support a wide range of stakeholders and facilitate long-term pandemic planning and recovery. This work draws on the authors' experiences in developing and deploying data-informed models for various stages of the pandemic response, including the tracking of cases and contacts, modeling disease transmission and recovery, and informing policy and personal decisions. We hope that our work will inspire a new generation of researchers to focus on the rapidly evolving field of pandemic data science, and to encourage a collaborative and inclusive approach to data governance and decision-making that prioritizes the needs of the most vulnerable populations. This approach will be essential in building a more resilient and adaptable global response to future pandemics. Voice conversion, a technique aimed at transforming one voice into another, has been a subject of research for decades. Recent advancements in diffusion-based generative models have yielded impressive results in natural-synthesis VC. However, existing approaches often require extensive training data and can only produce short utterances, making them impractical for real-world applications. This study presents DiffSVC, a novel diffusion-based VC model that can effectively learn a voice transfer function from a limited amount of target data even in a fully unsupervised setting. By utilizing a diffusion scheme with a flexible training duration, DiffSVC can process arbitrary-length audio, making it a more suitable choice for real-world applications. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that DiffSVC achieves comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art in voice conversion, using either a large training dataset or minimal target data. Furthermore, DiffSVC outperforms existing models in natural-synthesis VC even when only a small amount of target data is available. Despite this, existing approaches still struggle to adapt to novel situations, a key issue we aim to address. Our method, a key contribution, is distinct in its ability to learn meta-adjustments without requiring the entire dataset, instead utilizing only a few samples. Moreover, we provide insights into the learned meta-adjustments, shedding new light on the key factors influencing task adaption. In medical image analysis, the availability of extensive labeled data is often restricted. To address this limitation, we suggest a novel, unsupervised domain adaptation method that utilizes disentangled representations and graph convolutional networks for cross-domain image segmentation. By leveraging this approach, we can derive features that are disentangled into semantic and non-semantic components, and a graph neural network can be trained to predict semantic features while learning to reconstruct the input images from these features and random noise for the latent variables. Following disentanglement, we train a GCN to predict target domain labels from the extracted semantic features. This approach has been effectively applied to various medical image datasets, including MR and CT scans, for the purposes of unsupervised domain adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our method in achieving high performance in cross-domain image segmentation tasks. This research examines the possibility of employing active inference to guide
reinforcement learning. By leveraging the free energy principle, active inference
enables an agent to develop a comprehensive understanding of its environment,
including its dynamics and reward system, through minimal environmental interaction.
Our study merges active inference with model-free reinforcement learning, allowing
the agent to simultaneously explore the environment and acquire knowledge about
its rewards. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in a simple scenario where
a reward function is unknown and evolve-forward-guided random walks become a
competitor to traditional reinforcement learning techniques. Our findings suggest that
active inference offers a promising framework for reinforcement learning. The code
for this project is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository 'RL-AI' on github.com.

The task of segmenting an audio signal into sound events is a crucial yet underdeveloped challenge within the machine listening domain, with most current methods relying on time-consuming and computationally intensive processes. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel end-to-end segmentation approach that integrates end-to-end learning with a single, efficient operation inspired by YOLO. This method leverages a signal-to-signal convolutional neural network, a unique form of data augmentation, and a novel loss function to achieve superior performance. By applying this technique, we significantly surpass the performance of existing segmentation methods, with a notable improvement of 5% average F1 score, while also demonstrating exceptional classification capabilities in sound event detection tasks, outperforming top-rated classification models by 3-4 percentages. Additionally, our method boasts exceptional real-time capabilities, with a single inference executing at 30 frames per second on a standard GPU. These platforms often rely on a combination of optimization and simulation to achieve this goal. However, the initial design stage remains a largely unexplored area, particularly when it comes to incorporating user preferences. We demonstrate the potential of this method by applying it to design a bridge, and we also identify areas for further research to refine the approach. The outcomes of this study provide valuable insights that can be built upon for future advancements in generative design studies. This research introduces an innovative approach to the problem of social navigation, focusing on an agent interacting with multiple humans within a shared environment. We redefine the goal of social navigation as an optimization problem where the agent's primary objective is to secure a preferred position, while respecting the personal space and preferences of surrounding humans. To achieve this, we have developed a novel framework that incorporates a deep reinforcement learning method, paired with a novel reward function designed to empower humans within social interactions. Our experiments, conducted in both simulated and real-world settings, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in social navigation scenarios. Additionally, we have made our code and trained models publicly available to facilitate further research. For more details, see https://github.com/ozan-ozkan/socialnavigation. This research also includes a video showcasing the results, available at https://youtu.be/8s8s5s8. Moreover, we have conducted an ablation study to examine the impact of individual components on our proposed method's performance. Our experiments reveal that the preferred position of empowered humans within the environment is more likely to be occupied by the empowered agent. Furthermore, we have observed that the method with the empowerment component exhibits improved performance in terms of both reward and collision rates, compared to the method without the empowerment component. Finally, we have validated our proposed method's generalizability by applying it to real-world scenarios using a mobile robot equipped with RGB-D cameras. effectiveness and efficiency. Comparative analysis with existing techniques

To enhance semi-supervised learning, particularly for imbalanced datasets, we've developed an approach that integrates curriculum learning into the process. With FlexMatch, we can effectively align the difficulty levels of both labelled and unlabelled data, effectively addressing the issue of imbalanced learning. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach leads to significant improvements in the accuracy of image and text recognition tasks, including self-supervised learning and domain adaptation. Furthermore, we've found that FlexMatch can also be used to generate high-quality pseudo labels for other semi-supervised learning methods. As a result, we've achieved state-of-the-art performance in various image and text recognition tasks, including image classification ($\sim$1% improvement over previous best results), domain adaptation, and named entity recognition. This research introduces a novel approach for identifying heads in videos recorded within buildings, which poses significant challenges due to varying lighting conditions, different camera angles, and frequent view changes. To address this limitation, we developed a motion-aware pseudo Siamese network (MPSN) that can operate effectively with limited motion and minimal view changes. By incorporating a motion compensation module that predicts the motion field, we can simulate realistic motion scenarios, thus enabling the MPSN to accurately predict head motion and improve identification accuracy. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed MPSN, which outperforms other motion-based approaches in head identification, achieving a 2.5% improvement in mean average error. Additionally, the MPSN exhibits excellent generalization capabilities, as it can successfully identify heads in videos recorded with different cameras and view changes. Our work provides a comprehensive solution for head identification in videos, which can be applied to various surveillance scenarios. Traditional question-answering systems typically generate answers by selecting relevant information from a vast database and supporting their choices with underlying evidence. While this method is effective in retrieving accurate answers for many queries, it can sometimes lead to misleading results if the provided evidence is inaccurate or insufficient. To address this issue, we propose a new QA system that offers a step-by-step explanation for each answer, allowing users to evaluate the validity of each intermediate reasoning step and confidently rely on the final result. Our approach involves identifying the most probable causes for each fact mentioned in the evidence and transforming the process into a complex optimization problem. By solving this problem, our system can generate a coherent chain of reasoning that is grounded in truth and accurately answers the original question. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach produces reliable answers for a range of questions and maintains high accuracy even in the presence of noisy data. Furthermore, we found that our system's ability to provide transparent reasoning steps enhances users' understanding of the underlying facts and improves their ability to detect incorrect information. Overall, our research shows that making reasoning processes transparent and verifiable can lead to more reliable and trustworthy QA systems. We investigate the challenge of enhancing policies in a Constrained Markov Decision Process to maximize the expected cumulative reward, while adhering to constraints on the state-action occupancy counts. We develop a new algorithm that iteratively updates policies using the Frank-Wolfe method, incorporating dynamic reevaluation of constraint violations. We show that this algorithm rapidly converges to an approximate solution under mild conditions. Furthermore, a constraint-violation based termination criterion is provided to guarantee global convergence to the optimal policy. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a range of benchmark tasks. This research is the first to establish fast convergence of policy improvement algorithms in a Constrained Markov Decision Process setting. The developed algorithm can be applied to various problems involving constrained decision-making, such as task-oriented robotic manipulation, where it has shown promising performance. Programmers must balance the need to prevent data corruption with the necessity to prevent data loss due to premature deallocation. To address this, this paper introduces version-driven reclamation, an approach that safely and efficiently recovers memory allocated from programs that use speculative reclamation. The method relies on speculative reclamation's ability to record the version of allocated memory and uses a separate version counter to compare the versions of reclaimed and allocated memory. The proposed technique avoids overwriting memory that has not been deallocated by utilizing a simple and efficient comparison operation. Experimental results demonstrate that version-driven reclamation outperforms reference-based reclamation and that its overhead can be further reduced by applying it to specific memory regions, as demonstrated by its implementation in a Linux file system module. Notably, this approach eliminates the need to maintain a bitmap, which is typically used for detecting write conflicts in traditional reclamation methods. Moreover, the paper shows that version-driven reclamation can be integrated into existing software stacks without requiring any changes to existing reclamation algorithms. Traditional image restoration techniques often rely on piecewise uniform (pWI) priors, but these assumptions can be overly restrictive, leading to suboptimal results in real-world images. To address this issue, a novel continuous-domain two-stage regularization (T2CR) approach is proposed, which effectively captures the underlying pWI patterns in images. By modeling local variance as a continuous function, the method can efficiently handle various image types, including those containing noise, missing data, or multiple exponents. The T2CR approach consists of two stages: the first uses a total variation (TV) term to enforce sparsity in the wavelet domain, while the second stage employs a continuous-domain regularization (CDR) term to preserve local variance. The CDR term can be represented as a variational inequality problem and is efficiently solved using an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) framework. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on a range of image restoration tasks, including denoising, deblurring, and inpainting. Visual question answering (VQA) models typically struggle to generalize across new domains. To address this issue, researchers have developed domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge from a known domain to an unknown one. However, domain adaptation for VQA is often plagued by a major drawback: the need for a large dataset from the target domain, which is usually impractical to obtain. In this work, we propose a novel approach called Enhanced RAMEN, a self-supervised learning method that enables VQA models to generalize effectively to new domains without requiring a target domain dataset. Our method builds on RAMEN, a previous approach that used contrastive learning to learn generalizable visual representations. To enhance RAMEN, we introduce a contrastive learning objective that focuses on learning more robust object representations, and we also develop a new method for self-supervised learning that leverages the knowledge of pre-trained language models. Our experiments demonstrate that Enhanced RAMEN significantly outperforms RAMEN and other state-of-the-art approaches for domain generalization in VQA. Notably, Enhanced RAMEN achieves an impressive accuracy of 68.3% on the target domain, far exceeding the performance of RAMEN (60.4%) and other state-of-the-art approaches (e.g., 53.4% by DomainMix). Moreover, Enhanced RAMEN exhibits exceptional performance in zero-shot domain adaptation, achieving a remarkable accuracy of 59.3% on the unseen domain, surpassing the performance of RAMEN (45.4%) and other state-of-the-art approaches (e.g., 27.7% by DomainMix). Our results demonstrate that Enhanced RAMEN is a powerful tool for self-supervised learning in VQA, enabling models to generalize effectively to new domains without requiring a target domain dataset. This study introduces a novel controller that simulates human body characteristics to direct an aerial robot attached by a cable. The primary objective is to steer a human's hand along a predetermined path using physical interaction. The controller consists of two parts: the path tracking component and the human state controller. The path tracking controller employs a feedback control approach with a feedforward component based on the robot's trajectory, while the human state controller utilizes a disturbance disturbance reaction model to adjust the robot's trajectory in real-time according to the human's body dynamics. The human state controller is designed using a sliding mode controller, which is capable of estimating human body parameters from joint torque measurements. The efficacy of the proposed controller is demonstrated through simulations in various scenarios. The results reveal that the controller effectively adjusts the robot's trajectory in response to changes in human body parameters, such as increased stiffness, reduced mass, or altered human body dynamics. The controller also exhibits robustness to external disturbances and tracking errors, even when the robot experiences cable angle deviations. Furthermore, the results indicate that the controller's ability to estimate human body parameters facilitates improved performance in scenarios involving sudden changes in human body dynamics. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the development of safe and efficient human-robot collaboration systems. Additionally, our results indicate that the RL-based approach can be effectively applied to a range of matrix types, including those with singularities. Finally, we extend our method to the creation of local interpolation operators, enabling the development of a parallelizable AMG algorithm. In the context of Bayesian optimal transfer learning, we investigate the issue of estimating generalization errors. Our approach involves developing a novel variant of importance sampling and proposing a straightforward, effective algorithm for optimal Bayes transfer learning. This algorithm is characterized by its simplicity and computational efficiency. Specifically, its expected computational cost is directly proportional to the dimensionality of the action space and the number of samples used, and it only incurs a logarithmic cost in terms of the number of samples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the expected error of its approximation is closely linked to the smoothness of the objective function, and we establish a data-dependent error bound that is influenced by the empirical Bayes posterior and the prior. Our approach is validated through experiments on synthetic data and real-world tasks, including regression and reinforcement learning. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is capable of providing accurate error estimates for Bayes transfer learning, even in scenarios where the source and target domains are unrelated. Moreover, we show that the error bound is effective in distinguishing between well- and poorly matched transfer learning scenarios. Our work is the first to provide a comprehensive error analysis for Bayes optimal transfer learning. This paper examines the issue of reward tampering within the framework of reinforcement learning. We establish a causal diagram that encapsulates the problem's underlying dynamics, and subsequently identify two key scenarios. In the first instance, we establish a criterion for when a given reward function is deemed optimal for achieving a specified set of performance metrics. We subsequently propose a method for identifying such reward functions, and demonstrate that this approach is applicable to both continuous and discrete action spaces. In the second scenario, we explore the scenario where a reward function is unknown and the observed data originates from a system operating under a different reward mechanism. We develop a statistical framework for estimating the original reward function from this data. The validity of our approaches is demonstrated through both theoretical analysis and simulation-based testing. We also demonstrate the practical utility of these methods in the context of a reinforcement learning system that is capable of adaptively adjusting its reward function in response to changing environmental conditions. This adaptive reward adjustment is shown to be feasible in a range of scenarios, including the case where the environment's dynamics are unknown, the case where the reward function is unknown, and the case where the reward function is modified over time. We also examine the potential applications of these methods in the context of reward hacking within reinforcement learning systems. This exploration reveals that the methods developed here can be used to identify instances of reward hacking, and to prevent such behavior from occurring in the future. We also identify a range of potential applications for these methods in the context of reward tampering, including the case of malicious agents that are attempting to compromise the security of reinforcement learning systems. This compromise can occur in a range of different ways, including through the use of adversarial attacks, through the deployment of Trojan horses, and through the exploitation of vulnerabilities in the reward function. primarily used to model air showers in the transition from the upper atmosphere 
to the ground. The current version of CORSIKA 8 includes comprehensive 
implementations of hadronic interactions up to extremely high energies, 
along with detailed descriptions of shower development in the Earth's atmosphere. 
Various detectors and instruments can be simulated at the ground, allowing 
for extensive reconstruction of secondary particles and detection of secondary showers. 
To ensure accurate results, CORSIKA 8 has been validated through numerous 
comparisons with existing experimental data, with a particular emphasis on 
understanding uncertainties associated with hadronic interactions. 
In addition, the package has been optimized to enable users to model 
air showers in the presence of moonlight, with a specific focus on 
understanding the impact of Cherenkov light on these simulations. 
Lastly, the document highlights the ongoing development efforts in CORSIKA 8, 
including plans for future enhancements and upgrades to the package. 
These plans include integrating a new hadronic interaction model, 
enhancing the package's detector library, and expanding its physics capabilities. 
Ultimately, the goal of CORSIKA 8 is to provide a robust and accurate 
platform for scientists to model and analyze high-energy cosmic rays.

attending the ICRC 2021 conference and the broader community of scientists 
working with CORSIKA 8, with a particular emphasis on the contributions 
made by the authors at the conference.

In this research, we investigate how to teach an agent to navigate complex environments and adapt to changing conditions using reinforcement learning. We propose a novel framework called H-TRL, which enables an agent to learn from observations of its own behavior over time and adjust its actions accordingly. We introduce a novel technique for robotic manipulation of unknown objects based on a fundamental principle: objects naturally move in specific ways when an external force is applied, and by understanding these movements, we can match them to a well-established database of object behavior to predict their likely response to further interaction. This approach, which we call particle-driven object manipulation, enables the robot to learn about the object through a series of simple interactions, allowing it to adapt its strategy as needed to achieve the desired outcome. This method is highly effective, as it can handle a wide range of objects and environments, and can even learn to manipulate objects that are highly complex or unpredictable. Experimental results demonstrate the success of this approach on a variety of objects, including those made of fabric, rubber, paper, and others, and show that it can learn to solve complex problems in a highly efficient manner. Furthermore, this approach can be easily applied to a wide range of robotic tasks, including object manipulation, dexterous manipulation, and even learning to open doors. This makes particle-driven object manipulation a highly promising and versatile method for a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks. Our study presents a cutting-edge Bayesian U-Net method for automatically isolating moving ice and permanent ice on glaciers using Synthetic Aperture Radar imagery. The innovative approach leverages the strengths of a U-Net architecture paired with Bayesian inference to accurately distinguish the three components of a glacier system: moving ice, permanent ice, and everything else. To enhance the segmentation process, we incorporate a novel feature that utilizes the temporal characteristics of glaciers that are shrinking, making the moving ice component more distinct. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of the Bayesian U-Net method over other approaches, achieving an impressive 0.8 F1 score on a dataset of 12 icefields in Alaska, while the baseline U-Net method only achieved a score of 0.6. Our method was able to accurately identify the moving ice component in 11 out of 12 cases, even in scenarios where the icefields were experiencing significant melting. To verify the robustness of our approach, we also conducted experiments using simulated SAR imagery, which showed that the Bayesian U-Net method outperformed the baseline U-Net method by a margin of 0.2 in F1 score. Our method was also able to accurately identify the moving ice component in 11 out of 12 cases, even in scenarios where the icefields were experiencing significant melting. Our results demonstrate the potential of our approach for automatically isolating moving ice on glaciers using SAR imagery. Although graph neural networks have been applied to this field, they often fail to capture the inherent symmetries within molecular structures, leading to inconsistent predictions. In contrast, our proposed Equiformer model, a graph transformer network, ensures preservation of spatial and rotational symmetries, leveraging group equivariance to produce more accurate predictions. By integrating equivariant attention and equivariant multi-head attention mechanisms, Equiformer demonstrates superior performance in regression tasks, outperforming existing models like Graph Attention Networks and EquiTransformer on various chemical property prediction datasets. Our model's efficacy is further validated through ablation studies, highlighting the benefits of combined equivariant attention and equivariant multi-head attention mechanisms. Overall, our results indicate that Equiformer is a reliable choice for regression-based molecular property prediction tasks. Predicting future trajectories of individuals in complex scenes with varied
scenarios is a significant challenge. Current trajectory prediction models either
focus on a single scenario or lack the capacity to adapt to distinct scenarios.
In this paper, a novel approach is presented to address this challenge by
utilizing multiple trajectory templates that are tailored to diverse scenarios.
The proposed method, called MultiScenario Trajectory Prediction (MSTP), enables
models to adapt to various scenarios by selecting relevant trajectory
templates from a predefined library. By incorporating multi-scenario
predictors, MSTP outperforms existing approaches in multi-task prediction tasks
across multiple scenarios. Furthermore, extensive experiments demonstrate the
efficacy of MSTP in handling scenarios characterized by diverse behaviors and
traffic patterns. The source code for MSTP is available on GitHub.

In ALICE, UPC experiments involve detecting the collision of two nuclei, where one nucleus is always the lead nucleus (lead-lead or lead-gold) and the other is a lighter ion (proton, neutron, or a lighter nucleus like carbon or nitrogen). This approach is combined with Example-Guided Observation Prediction, which generates relevant example observations. To facilitate the exchange of information between intent and observation prediction, we propose a multi-task model that jointly trains both components. This approach is evaluated on two benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing intent and observation predictions. Hyperspectral images are a rich source of information that can be utilized in remote sensing applications, but their utility is compromised by noise contamination. This noise affects not only the visual quality of the images, but also the performance of subsequent tasks such as object detection and target recognition. To address this issue, a novel approach called SSCAN is proposed to denoise hyperspectral images by leveraging the underlying spatial-spectral relationships. SSCAN consists of two key components: a spatial-spectral fusion network that integrates spatial and spectral cues to predict noisy HSI pixels, and a recursive denoising module that progressively refines the clean HSI through iterative spatial-spectral denoising. By iteratively denoising the clean HSI, SSCAN can effectively eliminate noise while preserving spectral information. Furthermore, a novel cross-space network is designed to enhance spectral-spatial information and improve the denoising process. Experimental results on four real hyperspectral datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SSCAN in denoising hyperspectral images and outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, SSCAN has been integrated into a hyperspectral image denoising framework, which can be accessed through the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ChengyuLi/SSCAN. When these crystals are paired with low-temperature transition-edge sensor detectors, the resulting signals can be accurately measured. A recent study has shown that GaAs detectors with a low-temperature configuration have the potential to achieve a record-breaking dark matter detection limit of approximately $10^{-7}$ PG/cm$^2$ for a mass of 1 keV. This research aims to further optimize dark matter search capabilities by exploring the performance of GaAs and InAs detectors in a cryogenic environment. Computational modeling has been employed to simulate the performance of these detectors in a cryogenic setup, and the results indicate that GaAs and InAs detectors with a high energy resolution of better than 1 eV can be used to achieve a dark matter mass threshold of 1 keV. This work also examines the effects of detector resolution, background noise, and the potential for using cherenkov radiation to identify dark matter interactions. Ultimately, the findings suggest that combining GaAs or InAs detectors with a low-temperature transition-edge sensor technology has the potential to achieve a record-breaking dark matter detection limit of $10^{-7}$ PG/cm$^2$ for a mass of 1 keV. This research also indicates that such a setup can be used to study a wide range of masses from 1 keV to sub-keV levels. This work has the potential to significantly enhance the sensitivity of dark matter searches and open up new avenues for investigating dark matter. Future research directions include the development of advanced detector technologies that can be used to achieve even lower background noise levels and the potential for using these detectors in a variety of dark matter search experiments. This research has the potential to significantly enhance our understanding of the universe and the nature of dark matter. The problem of enhancing a viewing graph is defined as synchronizing multiple images to a common set of 3D points from multiple 2D image perspectives. This paper proposes a novel algorithm to resolve viewing graph enhancement while simultaneously determining object pose and movement. Initially, a cost function is formulated to optimize the transformation matrix, incorporating both translation and rotation to minimize occlusion and image distortion. This function is then combined with the cost function of feature matching to create an overall cost function. This cost function is used to develop an iterative algorithm that updates the transformation matrix and rotation/translation of each image. To improve the algorithm's efficiency, a novel method of dynamic elimination is introduced, removing unnecessary images from consideration. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superior accuracy compared to existing approaches. However, the traditional approach of using complete data streams can be inefficient due to the high storage requirements.  A new method called data stream fragmentation can reduce storage needs, dividing input data into smaller segments.  This study, known as MSRL, proposes a reinforcement learning framework that utilizes fragmented data streams and incorporates a novel agent design to handle the resulting data management challenges.  By leveraging the fragment information, the MSRL agent can effectively process the data and achieve better results.  The MSRL framework also incorporates a novel reward function that utilizes the fragment information to estimate the overall reward, and it demonstrates its ability to handle high-reward variability through a theoretical analysis.  The MSRL framework's performance is evaluated through a series of experiments using two real-world scenarios, and it outperforms existing methods in both scenarios.  Specifically, it achieves significant improvements in the multi-armed bandit problem and the reinforcement learning problem with high-reward variability. We investigate the disparity in variation between a stochastic differential equation featuring a local martingale and its approximate Gaussian version. The Gaussian approximation is applicable in situations where the drift and diffusion coefficients of the stochastic equation are of bounded variation. Our analysis focuses on jump times and their association with the variation in total variation between these times and the times of a Brownian motion. The key outcome of our research is the demonstration that the total variation disparity between the original equation and its Gaussian approximation is finite, provided that the original equation has stopping times. Furthermore, we establish that the total variation disparity between the original equation and its Gaussian approximation is proportional to the length of time elapsed. Our results are supported by numerical examples that demonstrate the convergence of the solutions to the original equation and its Gaussian approximation in total variation distance. Generative Adversarial Networks, specifically Wasserstein GANs with gradient penalty, have been widely used for image-to-image translation tasks. This paper reveals that these models are capable of solving a complex problem known as crowded p-transportation. In this process, multiple objects need to be rearranged in a container to minimize movement and congestion. Our findings show that optimizing the gradient penalty in WGANS actually solves the LP relaxation of this problem, enabling the arrangement of objects in an optimal way. This discovery opens up new research paths for image processing and container optimization. Moreover, we propose a novel approach to directly solve the original transportation problem, eliminating the need for its relaxed version. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in producing better solutions compared to the conventional linear assignment algorithm. Our work is expected to foster further research in the intersection of generative modeling and combinatorial optimization. We introduce a novel neural network that generates realistic neural radiance fields from a single image, incorporating a unique loss function that leverages the spatial arrangement of skin features to produce photorealistic portraits. Our approach, termed Portrait-NeRF, achieves accurate rendering of human portraits under varying lighting conditions, including realistic effects from occlusion, specularity, and micro-surface reflections. Our system effectively captures and reproduces the intricate structure and texture of human skin, including subtle wrinkles, hair color variations, and eyelid movements. To further evaluate and improve neural rendering capabilities, we also introduce a novel dataset of human portraits captured using cutting-edge 3D scanning technology, enabling the development of advanced portrait rendering techniques. Our experiments demonstrate that Portrait-NeRF consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural rendering methods, showcasing promising results. This paper features three open questions in real or real fractal geometry that we propose. We provide evidence that certain kinds of self-similar random fractals, only containing irrational numbers, are abundant within any given fractal family, yet not all. Furthermore, we show that a dense subset of an invariant random field under a scale transformation can consist of numbers that cannot be expressed as the quotient of integers, whereas the entire field is rational. Lastly, we examine the properties of certain self-similar positive random variables, focusing on the likelihood that their sum is a rational number. We identify specific criteria for this condition to hold, and also establish the existence of such variables with non-zero probabilities that a given sum equals a rational number. Additionally, we prove that a given class of positive random variables contains an infinite number of irrational sums, each of which can be expressed as the quotient of integers. The answers to these questions are derived from a combination of analytical and probabilistic methods. The paper also includes a comprehensive review of the relevant research background. As a secondary contribution, we provide a comprehensive answer to an open question first proposed by Jonsson and Vajda regarding the existence of certain kinds of self-similar positive random variables, originally posed in 2003. A significant challenge in machine learning is creating artificial agents that can learn and adapt in dynamic environments. To address this, researchers have developed a new approach that combines curiosity-driven exploration and task learning to enable artificial agents to discover and learn from non-equilibrium behaviors in complex systems. By utilizing a neural network to model the order parameter space of a system and incorporating a neural network-based reward function, the proposed method, called TaskNet, leverages intrinsic curiosity to encourage the agent to explore and learn dynamic behaviors. TaskNet has been applied to a range of complex systems, including a system of particles in a box and a system of particles interacting with a wall. Results show that TaskNet is capable of learning and adapting to non-equilibrium behaviors in these systems, including creating novel behaviors not seen during training. This approach offers a powerful framework for creating artificial agents that can learn and adapt in dynamic environments. Furthermore, the ability to learn and adapt non-equilibrium behaviors in complex systems, including those exhibiting phase transitions, suggests a range of potential applications for future research. Attribution methods are widely used to provide insights into how models make predictions and why they sometimes go wrong. However, existing attribution methods are often criticized for producing unstable and unreliable results. A recent study found that many popular attribution methods are sensitive to small changes in the model or the input, which can result in inaccurate explanations. Building on these findings, our research focuses on understanding how attribution methods work and how to make them more reliable. We propose a new metric called robustness, which measures a method's ability to produce consistent and stable results even when the model or input changes slightly. Through an exhaustive evaluation of 17 popular attribution methods on a wide range for different models, our analysis reveals that many popular attribution methods fall short in terms of robustness. Notably, our results show that some attribution methods, such as the DeepSHAP method, are highly sensitive to small changes in the model, while others, such as the Integrated Gradient method, are more robust. We also found that model ensembles can improve the robustness of attribution methods, but only if the models are already robust to small changes. Our research also identifies some attribution methods, such as the Gradient Activation Difference method, which are more robust than others. Finally, our results show that robust attribution methods are more reliable in their ability to detect adversarial attacks and can produce more accurate results even when the model is attacked. Our research provides a foundation for developing attribution methods that are more reliable and easier to trust. This research delves into compact and efficient setup configurations for distributed systems, specifically focusing on reducing the runtime setup overhead associated with parameter servers in machine learning. By introducing a novel method of compacting server configurations at compile-time, we enable the execution of multiple training processes with distinct parameters using a single, shared parameter server process. This approach allows for a more efficient use of memory and significantly reduces the frequency and magnitude of network communication between the parameter server and its clients, thereby accelerating training speed. We demonstrate the feasibility of this technique through a proof-of-concept implementation and showcase its potential benefits using a range of benchmark datasets. The results indicate a substantial reduction in training time, with a notable improvement in both single and distributed training settings. Although this technique may introduce additional overhead in the compilation process, the benefits in terms of training time far outweigh this minor inconvenience. By integrating this approach into the training pipeline, we can achieve a more efficient use of resources and accelerate training processes with minimal disruption. Furthermore, this technique can be easily adapted for use in other distributed training scenarios, thereby expanding its potential applications. By formulating the problem as a constrained optimization issue, the goal is to minimize state estimation error over time under a fixed privacy budget, and an efficient solution is derived using a dynamic programming approach. The solution is then enhanced with a real-time adaptation mechanism to optimize the private encoding mechanism. This research has significant implications for the study of magnetic ordering in systems with defects, as well as for the development of spin-based memory technologies. A new approach to pre-training is introduced for enhancing the performance of tasks related to Chinese video and language. Experimental results demonstrate that CVP achieves state-of-the-art results on various Chinese video and language tasks.
